name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: The AI Gateway for Calling 100+ LLM APIs
answer: LiteLLM is an open source AI gateway from BerriAI that lets you call over 100 LLM APIs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure and VertexAI, through one OpenAI-compatible interface, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It is written in Python with a Rust core being built for the proxy. The one thing to know before adopting it: it sits in the request path of every model call, so its reliability, memory use and upgrade discipline become your production concerns.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and is an AI gateway and Python library for calling large language model APIs. The repository is BerriAI/litellm, the language is Python, and the last recorded push is October 2026. It sits in the integration and routing layer of the AI stack, between your application and the model providers. Rather than teaching your code each provider's SDK and request format, you call LiteLLM and it translates to OpenAI format or native formats across more than 100 LLM APIs, including Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM. The official documentation is at docs.litellm.ai, and the project describes itself as the fastest, litest AI gateway, with a Rust core alongside the Python SDK.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are model routing and fallbacks, cost tracking and spend attribution, guardrails, load balancing, logging, and serving model traffic behind one endpoint. The documentation covers batch completion across many providers at once, reliability and load testing of providers, and a proxy that applies budgets and rate limits. It is strongest where a team needs one control plane over many providers and many callers: shared agents, per team budgets, key level limits, and audit trails. The blog describes an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway working together, with identity aware access and finance controls. For a single application calling a single provider, the gateway adds a hop you may not need.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for anyone who has called an LLM API, since the interface follows OpenAI conventions. The harder parts are operational rather than syntactic: running the proxy, configuring Redis, budgets, rate limits, teams and keys, and understanding retries and caching semantics. The official site offers tutorials, including reliability testing across providers, load testing endpoints, and visualization of results, plus a blog with incident reports and migration notes. It does not present itself as a teaching resource for machine learning fundamentals, so mathematics and model training knowledge are not prerequisites, while basic Python, HTTP and deployment familiarity are.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The facts record about 60,000 stars on the GitHub repository, which indicates a large and active user base. The documentation site spans roughly 60 pages covering tutorials, proxy configuration, budgets, guardrails and provider setup. The blog carries tags for ai-gateway and incident-report, with posts on Redis round trip reduction, a Rust gateway beta, and detailed postmortems. Integrations named in the material include Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM, Redis, and MCP servers with OAuth. The licence is listed as custom, so review its terms before commercial use. The site also describes LiteAdmin and a LiteAdmin MCP connector for managing the gateway through its management API.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends. The Python SDK is quick to adopt for experiments, and the proxy is built for production with budgets, guardrails, logging and multi team management. Performance is the active frontier: the blog reports the Python proxy peaking around 359MB of memory under load, and an early beta Rust gateway serving about 15 times the throughput, from 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11 times less memory, cutting per request overhead from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. The stated commitment is sub-1ms overhead and a sub-100MB binary. Those figures come from the project's own benchmark, so treat them as vendor measurements rather than independent results.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The material shows enterprise use: an enterprise customer running the database image behind nginx, teams sharing agents across business units, and Claude Code sessions routed through LiteLLM to Amazon Bedrock. The incident reports describe production outages and cost regressions affecting real deployments, which indicates the gateway is used in serious production paths rather than only in demos. The project is a current standard in the LLM gateway category, competing with Portkey and Bifrost in its own benchmark, and it is actively migrating to Rust. For someone choosing what to learn, gateway and LLM infrastructure skills are in demand, but the facts here do not quantify job market demand, so that judgment is yours to make.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is a Python project with a Rust core being built for the proxy, and it is typically used alongside application frameworks rather than replacing them. It calls providers over HTTP, using httpx for Mistral rather than the vendor SDK, and it exposes an OpenAI compatible interface so existing OpenAI client code can point at it. It integrates with Redis for caching and rate limiting, with MCP servers for tool access, and with identity providers through OIDC and OAuth. The polyglot pattern is a Python or other application calling the gateway, the gateway calling many providers, and a Rust binary eventually serving all traffic, with every hot path operation including auth and rate limiting running in Rust.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The documented weaknesses are operational. A September 2026 incident saw kernel OOM kills, one worker reaching 61GB RSS, and thousands of failed requests, caused by unbounded retry breadcrumbs combined with an unreachable Redis, and the fix was not backported before a stable tag. A July 2026 incident silently broke Anthropic prompt caching on Bedrock, raising spend two to three times with no error surfaced. The Rust gateway is an early beta, so its benchmark claims await independent verification. The licence is custom and the material does not explain its terms. The site does not state a supported version policy, a long term support window, or independent security audits, so those questions remain open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
